identity.label: About Han Che
identity.name: Han Che
identity.body: I connect the commercial, technical and human sides of change. Engineer, team lead and trainer, with 2,000+ hours of coaching and training.

about.readingKey: Read each case: before → intervention → result
about.contactTitle: Where is the work getting stuck?
about.closing: Start with the people, the process and the tools. Not another tool in isolation.
about.provenance: Selected first-person accounts, cross-checked against my CV and professional profile. These describe my contribution within teams, not independently audited results.

rib.title: A team that doesn't wait for its manager.

before.title: One gatekeeper
before.caption: Every decision queued behind one person.
before.body: Refinement, estimates, assignments and reviews converged on one gatekeeper. The team had too little ownership to move independently.

intervention.title: Shared decisions
intervention.caption: Shared planning, capacity and peer review.
intervention.body: I coached shared refinement and estimation, made capacity explicit and built peer review. Team members took responsibility for planning and their own Scrum rituals.

result.title: Independent team
result.caption: The team ran its own Scrum in ~5 months.
result.body: In ~5 months, the team was running its own Scrum rituals with little need for me to be in the room. Distributed ownership became daily practice.

rib.scope: About five months of team development. “Runs itself” refers to day-to-day team routines, not an organisation without leadership.
rib.note: My intervention was not another approval layer. I helped the team refine and estimate together, communicate its capacity and unblock work with other teams. Peer review gave colleagues a way to build agreement and carry decisions themselves.
rib.source: Basis: personal accomplishment notes; Engineering Manager role and five-month transformation recorded in my CV.

audi.title: Less meeting. More deciding.
audi.unit: minutes saved per meeting, on average

before.title: Legacy approval
before.caption: Brief: rebuild the Excel approval flow.
before.body: The final approval before serial production depended on a legacy process. The starting request was to reproduce the existing Excel workflow.

intervention.title: Model the process
intervention.caption: Stakeholder sessions became a state model.
intervention.body: With an architect colleague, I worked through stakeholder sessions, state diagrams and a relational data model. We built one core process end to end.

result.title: Digital sign-off
result.caption: A core-process demo, meetings 30 min shorter.
result.body: The core-process demo made the model tangible. The digitisation effort also shortened approval meetings by an average of 30 minutes.

audi.scope: 6–8 weeks refers to the working core-process demo. The initial release took 6 months. The 30-minute figure is the average meeting reduction, not a demo benchmark.
audi.note: State transitions gave stakeholders a model in their own domain language. The demo ran on pre-production with data import and export, side by side with the existing tool. It was a concrete basis for agreement on how the process should work.
audi.source: Basis: personal accomplishment notes for the demo; CV for the six-month initial release and average meeting reduction.

selfbits.title: Beyond the demo. Into production.

before.title: Production data
before.caption: Orders needed to become usable OEE data.
before.body: How can production orders become usable data about equipment effectiveness? The work needed to connect manufacturing processes with the people operating them.

intervention.title: Build and pilot
intervention.caption: Web, mobile and TV software, built and run.
intervention.body: I designed, implemented and operated manufacturing execution software with the team: web, mobile and TV interfaces for scheduling, master data and OEE.

result.title: Software in use
result.caption: 200+ users, 3 HEPA lines piloted in 9 months.
result.body: The software served 200+ users across the total deployment. A defined pilot acquired order-based OEE data on 3 HEPA lines in 2 factories within 9 months.

selfbits.scope: 5 factories and 200+ users describe the total deployment in my CV. The nine-month milestone covers the 3-line, 2-factory pilot, not the full rollout.
selfbits.note: Manufacturing execution software connects production planning with work on the factory floor. OEE means overall equipment effectiveness. Here, the pilot concerned acquiring that data per production order; no percentage improvement in OEE is claimed.
selfbits.source: Basis: CV for deployment and pilot scope; professional profile for work on scheduling, OEE dashboards and master data.

maintaining-markdown-for-ai.title: Maintaining markdown for AI
maintaining-markdown-for-ai.caption: AI collapsed the cost of writing documentation and raised the cost of verifying it. The work moved — and the verifying half is nobody else's job.
maintaining-markdown-for-ai.description: AI collapsed the cost of writing documentation and raised the cost of verifying it. Maintaining markdown for AI: where the effort goes and how to steer the machine half.

markdown-in-ai-workflows.title: Markdown in AI workflows
markdown-in-ai-workflows.caption: A single format carrying three of the six context types: Knowledge, Instructions, and Memory.
markdown-in-ai-workflows.prose: A plain text file with nothing mechanical underneath. What matters is how and when it is consumed: as knowledge, as instructions, as memory — and whether the agent pays for it on every turn or only when it reaches for it.

three-contexts.description: Markdown carries Knowledge, Instructions, and Memory with distinct lifecycle and retrieval costs.

retrieval-cost.description: What matters is whether the agent pays context tokens on every turn or retrieves on demand.

agentic-era.title: The agentic era
agentic-era.script: Before we start, I want to establish why markdown files matter so much in AI workflows. We're in the agentic era now — it isn't 2023 anymore. Agents aren't chatbots you copy-paste into. They read files on your machine, write files, call tools, search the web. Put those in a loop and they carry out real tasks, the way the new colleague you just onboarded would.

three-categories.title: Three categories of markdown
three-categories.script: And like that colleague, an agent needs the right information at the right time. That information lives in markdown — which is just a plain text file. Those files fall into three categories. Knowledge — what the agent looks up on demand, when the task calls for it. Instructions — skills: how to do a release, step by step, written once and called by name. And memory — not ChatGPT's memory, but a file the agent reads at the start of every single conversation. And if that file is stale, or wrong, the agent reads that wrong information every single time. Confidently, and silently — without you ever noticing.

volume-outruns-review.title: Volume outruns review
volume-outruns-review.caption: On one document, maintenance effort decays while drift climbs — that crossing is where the work moved. Across a corpus, the maintenance surface grows faster than the file count.
volume-outruns-review.prose: Two different things get harder. On a single document, maintenance effort decays while drift keeps climbing. Across a corpus, the maintenance surface grows faster than the file count.

decay-vs-drift.description: On a single document, maintenance effort decays while drift climbs — that crossing is where the work moved.

corpus-compounding.description: Across a corpus, the verification surface multiplies faster than the raw file count.

effort-decay.title: Effort decay and drift
effort-decay.keywords: decay curve, effort drops, drift climbs, maintenance budget
effort-decay.script: And that's one document. There's a reason knowledge management was always hard in enterprise — long before any of this. And it's this shape. One document, over time: the blue line is effort. There's a spike at the start, when someone writes it. At least, that's how it used to be — with AI, creating a document now costs almost nothing. After that, effort drops. Because nobody budgets for maintenance. It's never in the plan. And as effort drops, drift climbs. The document is still sitting there. It's just quietly stopped being true.

corpus-compounding.title: Corpus compounding
corpus-compounding.keywords: accumulate steadily, claims and references, brake is gone
corpus-compounding.script: Now scale that. Your documents don't arrive one at a time — they accumulate, steadily. And you're not just verifying each file. You're verifying every claim each file makes about the others. Every reference. That compounds. So here's what changed: writing was the brake. The human was the bottleneck — you could only produce documentation as fast as someone could write it, and that held the whole thing in check. That brake is gone.
corpus-compounding.bridge: So the brake is gone. Which raises the obvious question: what does it actually take to check a document?

where-the-effort-goes.title: Where the effort goes
where-the-effort-goes.caption: What a machine can check, what AI can help with, and what only a human can check.
where-the-effort-goes.prose: Three boundaries: what a machine automates, what AI accelerates, and what only a human can decide.

three-boundaries.description: Document verification is three distinct jobs: deterministic machine checks, AI acceleration, and human judgment.

division-of-labour.description: Push mechanics to the machine and discovery to AI so humans only handle genuine judgment calls.

three-boundaries.title: Three non-interchangeable tiers
three-boundaries.keywords: machine, human, AI, deterministic to semantic
three-boundaries.script: It's not one job. It's three, and they're not interchangeable. On the left, the machine: deterministic — same input, same answer, every time. Binary: it passes or it fails. Cheap, and fast. This is the part you want doing as much as possible. On the right, the human: not deterministic, slow, expensive. This is where the semantic work happens — is this actually true, is it still useful. And it's still where almost all trust comes from. And in the middle, AI: it works in natural language, so it sits on the human side of that line — not deterministic. It costs tokens. What it can and can't be trusted with is genuinely unsettled.
three-boundaries.bridge: Left to right. Cheap and certain, to expensive and human. Let's take them in order.

what-the-machine-verifies.title: What the machine verifies
what-the-machine-verifies.caption: Syntactic and structural checks that run deterministically in milliseconds without an LLM.
what-the-machine-verifies.prose: Syntax parses, URI format is validated, and ISO dates validate.

deterministic-checks.description: Syntax, schemas, dates, and URIs validate deterministically in milliseconds without an LLM.

mechanical-ceiling.description: A clean pass proves structural integrity, never that the underlying statement is true.

mechanical-ceiling.title: What the machine verifies
mechanical-ceiling.keywords: frontmatter, metadata shape, link checker, ceiling
mechanical-ceiling.script: Start with the low-hanging fruit. What can a machine check, every time, for free? Here's a markdown file — an onboarding process. At the top, the frontmatter: key-value pairs in YAML that carry metadata, mostly for the machine and the agent. Underneath, the body. A machine can check the shape of that metadata. Is the type declared. Is the date a real date. Is the link well-formed — and it can even follow it and see if it's still there. And that's the ceiling. It can tell you the field exists. It can't tell you whether what's written in it is true.

what-ai-accelerates.title: What AI accelerates
what-ai-accelerates.caption: Cross-referencing prose against source handbooks to flag discrepancies for human review.
what-ai-accelerates.prose: The answer comes back rapid, insightful, and itself in need of checking.

cross-referencing.description: AI can follow references across files and flag contradictions for human review.

signals-not-resolutions.description: The AI recommendation is rapid and insightful, but remains an unverified claim itself.

signals-and-contradictions.title: What AI accelerates
signals-and-contradictions.script: So what does AI add? It can follow that reference. Read the document on the other end. And notice that this one says five days and that one says seven. That's a contradiction it found on its own — and what it does with it matters more than finding it. It can flag that one section and raise a ticket, so a human resolves a single line instead of re-reading the document. Those are signals. Every signal narrows what a human actually has to look at. But can it make the call? It can produce one. It's like stopping someone in the street, handing them both documents, and asking which is right. You'll get an answer. If you own this process — would you trust that person?

what-remains-human.title: What remains human
what-remains-human.caption: Is the policy still in force? Is the owner correct? Ground truth that no machine or model can know.
what-remains-human.prose: This judgment stays open on screen.

ground-truth.description: Whether a policy is active or an owner is correct requires ground truth outside the repository.

accountability.description: Tooling narrows the decision surface, but accountability stays with the human.

accountability-ground-truth.title: What remains human
accountability-ground-truth.script: Which leaves this: is the coffee thing still how the team works? Is this person still the owner? No amount of tooling answers those. You have to know — and you're the one accountable when it's wrong. The machine narrows it. The AI narrows it further. What's left is the part that was always yours.

google-okf.title: Google OKF
google-okf.caption: Full OKF v0.2 frontmatter schema governing provenance, trust, and lifecycle.
google-okf.prose: A standardized frontmatter schema to govern AI knowledge bases. Provenance, trust tiers, and lifecycle fields sit directly in markdown alongside the content.

open-knowledge-format.description: OKF v0.2 standardizes frontmatter fields for AI knowledge bases.

lifecycle-fields.description: Provenance, trust tiers, and lifecycle sit directly in markdown next to the content.

shared-vocabulary.title: Google Open Knowledge Format
shared-vocabulary.keywords: OKF v0.2, shared vocabulary, agent generated human verified, lifecycle
shared-vocabulary.script: The machine finds structure. The AI adds a first layer of meaning, to help a human decide faster. And what's left was always yours. So let's go back to the machine half, and ask how we make it bigger. A machine works on structure. Which means it only works if we agree on a shared vocabulary. This is Google's Open Knowledge Format. It's open, and it's early — version 0.2, still moving. It names the fields, and says what each one means: type, title, description, sources, and the interesting ones: trust, and lifecycle. That a document was generated by an agent, and verified by a human. And stale_after — freshness. If we all agree to use the same vocabulary, the checker gets written once, and works everywhere.
shared-vocabulary.bridge: Which makes the machine's half a lot bigger than checking that a date is a date.

steering-the-ai.title: Steering the AI
steering-the-ai.caption: markdown-harness steers the machine half
steering-the-ai.prose: A document can tell you how much of itself to believe. Not full trust — a floor that holds, and a reliable signal when a human needs to act.

raising-the-floor.description: A document can declare how much of itself to believe; reliable signals warn when humans must step in.

tool-boundary.description: markdown-harness steers the machine layer and prepares signals without claiming human judgment.

raising-the-floor.title: Steering the AI
raising-the-floor.keywords: markdown-harness, raise floor, steer arrow, human boundary
raising-the-floor.script: So the goal is to make the machine's half do more. And this is what I've been building over the past couple of weeks: markdown-harness. The idea is one sentence: a document can tell you how much of itself to believe. It's not about generating trust. Trust is semantic — a machine can never produce it. What it can do is raise the floor. Reliable signals that tell an agent or a human that something needs attention. You've seen these three circles before: deterministic, cheap, fast signals handed to the AI while it's working. The machine column reaching into the AI column. That's the arrow. And the human side is greyed out on purpose: this tool stops before it. That part was always yours.

deterministic-core.title: Runs on a 100% deterministic core
deterministic-core.caption: One mechanism, three triggers, one deterministic core.
deterministic-core.prose: Three things can start it and it does three different things with the answer. What happens in between is the same every time.

three-triggers.description: Pre-read agent hook, pre-commit gate, or manual check all execute the identical deterministic core.

predictable-eval.description: Configuration and file inputs produce the exact same verdict every run.

three-triggers.title: One deterministic core
three-triggers.keywords: three triggers, runtime pre-read, commit gate, nightly schedule
three-triggers.script: Three ways in. Three ways out. And the middle is the same every time. Whatever starts it, the core does one thing: read the configuration, run the logic. Same input, same answer. It's fully deterministic. The one I want to show you is the first: the agent goes to read a file — and before it does, it's told that file is stale. The other two, briefly: on commit, a check that the frontmatter meets the standard, passing or blocking. And on a schedule: a nightly run that regenerates what can be regenerated, and raises a ticket on what can't.
three-triggers.bridge: Let me show you the first one.

live-demo.title: Live demo
live-demo.caption: The check, run live.
live-demo.prose: File under test: docs/handbook/onboarding.md. Asked of the agent: What are the first-week onboarding steps for a new hire?

demo-contrast.description: Three agents receive the same stale document; only the hooked agents are prevented from hallucinating outdated facts.

holding-slide.description: Talk switches to terminal here; the slide acts as the anchor framing the test.

demo-walkthrough.title: The check run live
demo-walkthrough.keywords: three terminals, un-hooked, pirate injection, deny read
demo-walkthrough.script: Three panels: same question, same document. The only difference is what each one is allowed to know. Before the run: watch the un-hooked panel answering confidently from a document that went out of date. If it noticed the date, that detection was luck — dependent on the model. The injected panel: the pirate response proves the harness governed what the agent was allowed to know. The deny panel: read was refused explicitly. And deterministic detection was recorded in the log, independent of what any model chose to say.

feature-roadmap.title: Feature Roadmap
feature-roadmap.caption: Three shipped, three planned.
feature-roadmap.prose: v0.0.4 Shipped: frontmatter linting, staleness checking, markdown harness skill.

v0-0-4-scope.description: Shipped: frontmatter linting, staleness checks, and markdown-harness skill.

future-checks.description: Future: drift detection and corpus validation; do not promise them as shipping today.

the-verifying-half-is-yours.title: The verifying half is yours
the-verifying-half-is-yours.caption: Back to the Venn, with the human region lit and the rest dimmed. Nothing new to read.
the-verifying-half-is-yours.prose: The work moved. It moved to you.

the-work-moved.description: Writing docs is automated; verifying them is the real work, and it belongs to you.

closing-thesis.description: Machines verify structure, AI accelerates cross-references, and human judgment owns accountability.

closing-thesis.title: The verifying half is yours
closing-thesis.keywords: third time, lit human region, work moved, always yours
closing-thesis.script: This is the third time you've seen this picture. First as what verification costs. Then as what the tool does — reaching into the middle, and stopping at the edge of the human. Same three circles. All that's changed is which one is dark. Machines check structure. AI accelerates drafting. And the work moved — to the part that was always yours. One thing I want to be straight about: the middle region is my hypothesis. How much an agent can be trusted with is not settled — an open problem. The tool's here if you want it. It's early. Thank you.

ai-token-economy.title: The AI Token Economy
ai-token-economy.caption: AI can give you and the people you lead super powers, but it comes with hidden managing responsibilities you didn't sign up for.
ai-token-economy.description: A field guide to the token economy: what AI actually costs, why the meter stays invisible, and how to manage context and models efficiently.

motivation.title: Motivation
motivation.caption: Thought experiment: Imagine you're assigned a freelancer with these weird characteristics.
motivation.prose: On paper, this collaborator arrives with encyclopedic knowledge, works instantly, and accepts tasks without hesitation. But they carry three peculiar flaws.

freelancer-metaphor.description: Translates abstract LLM mechanics into intuitive human management terms: encyclopedic knowledge, instant execution, but crucial blind spots.

management-opt-in.description: Treating an LLM as a teammate requires recognizing its failure modes rather than treating it as an infallible search oracle.

lead-one-upskill-many.title: Lead One, Upskill Many
lead-one-upskill-many.caption: It's an LLM — but if it were a human, how would you manage it?
lead-one-upskill-many.prose: Directing an AI agent requires the same delegation and review rigor as onboarding an external specialist.

upskill-vs-replace.description: The objective is not replacing workers but elevating human operators into effective directors of synthetic labor.

the-four-eras-of-ai.title: The Four Eras of AI
the-four-eras-of-ai.caption: New technology gives rise to new disciplines for humans to cope.
the-four-eras-of-ai.prose: From Prompt Engineering in 2023 to Context Engineering in 2024, Harness Engineering in 2025, and Token Economics today.

emerging-disciplines.description: As model capabilities advance, operational focus shifts from prompt words to managing context, harnesses, and token budgets.

the-invisible-invoice.title: The Invisible Invoice
the-invisible-invoice.caption: For a real freelancer you need a business case. AI just bills you.
the-invisible-invoice.prose: A €3,200 consultant invoice requires purchase orders and approvals. AI accumulates identical costs silently across thousands of micro-prompts.

governance-asymmetry.description: Corporate finance demands formal approval for contractors, yet AI charges comparable budgets without procurement gates.

outcome-per-euro.title: Outcome Per Euro
outcome-per-euro.caption: You're now accountable for a budget you never signed up to manage.
outcome-per-euro.prose: Defaulting to flagship frontier models for routine chores burns capital. The economic winner optimizes outcome per euro.

budget-accountability.description: Selecting the right tier for each task is the foundation of modern engineering leadership.

what-is-a-token.title: What Is a Token
what-is-a-token.caption: Tokens are the basic unit of data for LLMs — every one is billed.
what-is-a-token.prose: LLMs calculate statistical probabilities over numerical tokens. Every word, character, and prompt translates to billable units.

probabilistic-units.description: LLMs process numerical token IDs, not human prose. Understanding token granularity reveals where costs accumulate.

live-context-breakdown.title: Live Context Breakdown
live-context-breakdown.caption: Most tools hide the meter — this is what seeing it looks like.
live-context-breakdown.prose: A typical 200k session breakdown: system prompts, conversation history, tool payloads, and retrieved documentation.

synthetic-abstractions.description: Commercial interfaces conceal real token usage behind credits and bars. Direct transparency is essential for optimization.

cli-vs-web-tool-obscurity.title: CLI vs Web Tool Obscurity
cli-vs-web-tool-obscurity.caption: The meter is hidden on purpose.
cli-vs-web-tool-obscurity.prose: Obscurity is a product pattern: frictionless initiation, habitual workflows, and surprising monthly invoices.

the-obscurity-playbook.description: Hiding usage metrics fosters dependency before organizations realize the compounding cost of unmanaged agentic loops.

managing-context.title: Managing Context
managing-context.caption: Context window is the model's attention span.
managing-context.prose: Tokens accumulate in the context window. As the window fills, attention degrades and critical instructions slip away.

cognitive-stamina.description: Context windows behave like cognitive stamina across a long workday: alert early on, distracted as history piles up.

the-lost-middle.title: The Lost Middle
the-lost-middle.caption: How key instructions get lost in the middle.
the-lost-middle.prose: Models attend sharply to the start and end of context, but the middle blurs into an attention valley.

attention-valley.description: Research proves the U-shaped retrieval curve: information placed in the middle of long contexts suffers dramatic recall drops.

the-fullness-gauge-and-levers.title: The Fullness Gauge & Levers
the-fullness-gauge-and-levers.caption: Past ~half full, the model starts losing the plot.
the-fullness-gauge-and-levers.prose: Below 50% is the smart zone. Above 50%, accuracy degrades. Above 75%, hallucination risk spikes. Three levers: Monitor, Compact, Hand off.

smart-zone-discipline.description: Keeping context windows under 50% capacity guarantees high accuracy and prevents silent prompt drift.

cost-of-agentic-ai.title: Cost of Agentic AI
cost-of-agentic-ai.caption: One small bug fix compounds to ~73,000 tokens of context.
cost-of-agentic-ai.prose: Agentic loops re-transmit the entire conversation history on every single tool call and reflection step.

agentic-compounding.description: Each tool call and test run appends full file outputs into history, compounding input token counts exponentially.

the-compounding-cost-curve.title: The Compounding Cost Curve
the-compounding-cost-curve.caption: The same bug fix, priced across models.
the-compounding-cost-curve.prose: You are billed for tokens processed on every turn, not window capacity. A routine bug fix produces a 14× price swing across models.

the-14x-spread.description: At scale, routing identical loops between frontier and economy tiers creates a multi-thousand-dollar difference each month.

model-tiers.title: Model Tiers
model-tiers.caption: My real model stack: one workflow, many models.
model-tiers.prose: Route each phase to the most economical capable model: flat-rate chats for ideation, frontier reasoning for architecture, fast models for code execution.

tiered-stack-architecture.description: Economic fluency means matching engine cost to task risk, switching models seamlessly as project phases progress.

zero-marginal-thinking.description: Use flat-rate consumer subscriptions for exploratory chats, reserving pay-per-token frontier calls for high-leverage decisions.

tools-and-tips.title: Tools & Tips
tools-and-tips.caption: Three levers to improve your token economy
tools-and-tips.prose: Combine automated tooling (rtk, compression, linting) with structural context steering and disciplined team habits (edit don't append, session hygiene).

tooling-and-steering.description: Automated compressors prune tool payloads before they reach the model, while structured rules steer execution deterministically.

operational-habits.description: Edit flawed prompts instead of stacking corrections, clear idle sessions before cache expiry, and monitor usage via transparent CLIs.

talkPlayer.subtitle: Your AI reads stale docs every time · 22 min
talkPlayer.heading: THE TALK
